candidate.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: perform focused screening and assessments that identify aspiration risk and complications before initiating care activities that could increase harm.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — post-stroke dysphagia screening before oral intake
candidate.educational_objective: Before oral intake after acute stroke, use the facility's validated dysphagia-screening process to identify swallowing risk and trigger further evaluation when needed while recognizing that screening reduces risk but does not guarantee prevention of aspiration or pneumonia.

options.A: Complete an approved bedside dysphagia screen before oral intake; if the screen is abnormal, restrict oral intake and arrange further swallowing evaluation according to the stroke protocol.
options.B: Offer a small amount of water first because formal screening has little role in identifying aspiration risk after stroke.
options.C: Skip dysphagia screening if the client speaks clearly because swallowing impairment occurs only when aphasia is present.
options.D: Assume that passing a bedside screen guarantees that aspiration and hospital-acquired pneumonia cannot occur.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline states that bedside dysphagia screening before oral intake has inherent clinical logic because it can identify patients at risk, guide additional definitive swallowing assessment, and inform nutritional management. Observational data suggest screening may reduce pneumonia, but the guideline also emphasizes that screening does not prevent every episode of aspiration or hospital-acquired pneumonia and that no single screening method has been proven superior. B initiates oral intake before screening. C falsely links dysphagia only to aphasia. D overstates the protective value of a passed screen.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Post-stroke dysphagia screening before oral intake can identify patients at risk and guide further swallowing/nutritional evaluation; it may reduce pneumonia risk but does not guarantee prevention of aspiration or pneumonia and no single screening method is universally superior.
candidate.source_document_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
candidate.source_locator: Section 5.2 Dysphagia — Synopsis: bedside screening may help prevent aspiration and pneumonia through early identification of at-risk patients, but screening/formal evaluation/oral-intake restrictions do not prevent all aspiration or hospital-acquired pneumonia. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text 1–3: there is inherent logic in screening for dysphagia before oral intake; screening may reduce pneumonia in observational studies, guide additional definitive testing, and aid nutritional management; no specific screening method has proven superiority.
